records.value: We can now describe how stomata open and close: ion and water movement change the shape of the guard cells. In Lesson 1 gas escaped from specific spots, and stomata are the likely exits. • Tube A (air available): 5 mL ordinary warm water + 1 g dry yeast + 2 g glucose (sukari), shaken well so that air is mixed in → stoppered, with a delivery tube leading to a test tube of fresh limewater.
• Tube B (air kept out): 5 mL boiled-and-cooled water + 1 g dry yeast + 2 g glucose (sukari), stirred gently → a 1 cm layer of cooking oil poured gently on top to keep air out → stoppered, with a delivery tube leading to a separate test tube of fresh limewater.

records.value: Warmth speeds up respiration in yeast (and in plant cells) by speeding up enzyme-controlled reactions, until the temperature is high enough to damage the enzymes. This is a rate effect that builds over minutes. It does not by itself explain why bubbles stream from a sukuma wiki leaf within seconds of being put in warm water. That question goes to Lesson 8, where the class separates the quick physical effect of warmth on gas from the slower effect on respiration.
records.old: The anchoring phenomenon of more bubbles from sukuma wiki in warm water than in cold water can now be explained quantitatively: warmer temperatures increase the kinetic energy of respiratory enzyme molecules and their substrates, increasing the frequency of successful enzyme-substrate collisions in the glycolysis and Krebs cycle pathways, thereby increasing the rate of CO2 production and the number of bubbles observed — directly linking cellular enzyme kinetics to the visible macroscopic phenomenon first observed in Lesson 1.

records.value: By Lesson 8, students have gathered evidence about stomatal structure and function, gas exchange pathways, lenticels, cuticle, pneumatophores, aerobic respiration, and anaerobic respiration. This synthesis lesson draws all those threads together and returns to the Lesson 1 bubbles with better tools. The gas inside a leaf is a shared pool: stomata let it move in and out, photosynthesis adds O₂ and removes CO₂ in the light, and respiration adds CO₂ and removes O₂ all the time. Students separate what pushes gas out of a leaf quickly in warm water (the gas expands and dissolves less) from what photosynthesis and respiration change slowly (the mix of O₂ and CO₂ in the leaf's air). They revise their unit models and update the Driving Question Board to capture what is now understood versus what still needs investigation.

records.value: Signal the start of investigations: 'You have 40 minutes. Your job is to collect honest data — that includes results that do not match your prediction. Anomalies are valuable evidence, not mistakes. Begin.' Circulate continuously using a structured rotation: spend approximately 4–5 minutes at each group, then move on. Use the following specific prompts during circulation — (1) Variable control check: 'Show me what you are keeping constant. How are you making sure the amount of yeast, the water temperature and the bottle size are the same across your trials?' (2) Data recording check: 'Is every reading going straight into your table? I should see units in the column headers.' (3) Anomaly probe: 'That reading looks different from the others. Before you cross it out, ask yourselves — could that be real? What might have caused it?' Allow 10 seconds of WAIT TIME after each probe. (4) Mechanism prompt: 'You are seeing [observation]. Which process from our lessons explains why that might be happening?' Cold-call a non-recording group member to answer (aim to cold-call at least 3 different students per group visit across the lesson). Troubleshooting for the teacher: if a yeast mixture gives no gas, check that the water was not hot (above about 50°C kills yeast) and that the yeast is in date; if a balloon does not inflate, check the neck for leaks; plain maize flour gives few bubbles because yeast cannot use starch directly (this is why busaa brewers sprout the grain first) — treat it as a result to explain. For Tracks B and C, make sure each group has day-0 readings, labels the set-up with the group name and date, and writes who will do the 2-minute daily check; store the set-ups away from flames and out of the sun, with outlet tubes open. At the 20-minute mark, call a 2-minute 'Data Pause': all groups stop, look at their data so far, and write one sentence in their notebook: 'The pattern I am seeing so far is…' During the pause, send one learner from each group to count the bubbles in one of the five shared beakers for 1 minute and write the class counts on the board. Expected result (not guaranteed; accept what the leaves show): the no-leaf beaker gives few bubbles; the beaker with only the cut edges coated gives fewer bubbles than the untreated leaf; coating the lower surface cuts the count more than coating the upper surface. If the counts are messy (they often are), say so: 'This is real data. What might have affected it — leaf age, size of the piece, water temperature?' At the 35-minute mark, prompt groups to repeat a measurement or to calculate means if two trials are complete.

Separately, warmth speeds up enzyme-controlled respiration (shown with yeast) and photosynthesis (when there is light), which change the leaf's gas mix more slowly. Plants exchange gases not only through stomata but also through the cuticle, lenticels on woody stems, and pneumatophores in waterlogged environments. Inside cells, aerobic respiration (in the mitochondria) releases much more energy per glucose than anaerobic respiration (in the cytoplasm): aerobic respiration gives CO₂ and water, and anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells gives ethanol and CO₂, or lactic acid in some bacteria and in animal muscle. records.value: The sukuma wiki leaves were not 'breathing' at random. The specific spots from which bubbles emerged are openings of the leaf: stomata, whose size is regulated by guard cells through changes in turgor pressure driven by potassium ion (K⁺) movement and osmosis, and cut edges. records.old: The sukuma wiki leaves were not 'breathing' randomly — they were performing precisely regulated, enzyme-driven metabolic processes at the cellular level. records.value: (a) Warming makes gas expand: the air in the leaf's air spaces takes up more room, so some is pushed out through the stomata and cut edges. Warm water also holds less dissolved gas, so dissolved air comes out as bubbles. In cold water the air expands less and the water holds more gas, so fewer bubbles form. (b) Respiration makes carbon dioxide (it needs glucose and, in aerobic respiration, oxygen). Photosynthesis makes oxygen (it needs light, carbon dioxide and water). Both are controlled by enzymes and work over minutes: our yeast limewater took several minutes to turn cloudy, but the leaf bubbles started within seconds. So these processes cannot make most of the gas in the first bubbles; most of it was air already in the leaf and in the water. We did not test the gas from the leaf (for example with limewater), so we cannot be certain of its contents. 'Mostly air from the leaf's air spaces' is our best-supported explanation, and respiration and photosynthesis would change the proportions of oxygen and carbon dioxide only slowly. (c) The Lesson 6 investigation tested temperature: yeast in warm sugar-cane juice produced more CO₂ bubbles per minute than yeast in cold water, and the rate fell again at 55°C when the enzymes were damaged. Enzymes work faster when warmer because molecules move faster and collide more often, so respiration speeds up, but over minutes. The Lesson 4 limewater test compared air available with air kept out; it did not test temperature. The balloon bottles with different amounts of yeast showed that more yeast gave faster gas production but did not vary temperature. The Lesson 10 shared bubble counts (petroleum jelly on different surfaces and on the cut edges) tested where the gas escapes, not what the gas is.
records.old: (a) Respiration and photosynthesis are controlled by enzymes. In warm water the enzyme molecules and their substrate molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more often, so more reactions succeed each second. More gas is produced and more bubbles appear. In cold water the enzymes work slowly, so little gas is made and few bubbles appear. (b) Carbon dioxide is made by cellular respiration in the mitochondria of mesophyll cells. Oxygen is made by photosynthesis in the chloroplasts, but this needs light, so it only happens if the submerged leaf is lit. Some CO2 from respiration would also dissolve in the water, so fewer CO2 bubbles would be seen than the amount actually made. We did not test the bubbles from the leaf (for example with limewater), so we cannot be certain of their contents. Our best explanation, based on the yeast evidence and what we know about leaf cells, is that the bubbles are mostly gas released from leaf cells and air spaces through the stomata, with CO2 from respiration and, in light, O2 from photosynthesis possibly contributing. (c) The Lesson 6 investigation tested temperature: yeast in warm sugar-cane juice produced significantly more CO2 bubbles per minute than yeast in cold water, so respiration rate increased with warmth, matching the sukuma wiki pattern. The Lesson 4 limewater test compared aerobic and anaerobic conditions, not temperature, so it shows that respiration makes CO2 but does not itself show the temperature effect (though warming also made the limewater turn milky faster). The balloon bottles with different yeast concentrations also inflated because of CO2 from yeast, showing that more yeast gave faster gas production, but they did not vary temperature. So the Lesson 6 data support the idea that temperature controls respiration rate through enzyme activity.

records.old: The bubbles come from stomata, microscopic pores in the leaf surface, which is why they appear at specific spots and not over the whole leaf. Guard cells open each pore when K+ ions enter and water follows by osmosis, making them turgid. The gas in the bubbles comes from the leaf's cells and air spaces and leaves through the open stomata. Two gases are made in the leaf: carbon dioxide, made by aerobic respiration in the mitochondria of mesophyll cells (glycolysis, Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, giving about 36 to 38 ATP per glucose), and oxygen, made by photosynthesis in the chloroplasts, but only if the submerged leaf receives light. Because some CO2 dissolves in the water, the bubbles may contain relatively less CO2 than the leaf produces. We did not test the leaf bubbles directly, so this is our best explanation from the evidence of the unit rather than a proven fact. Warm water (about 42°C) gave more bubbles than cold water (about 15°C) because higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of enzymes and substrates, so enzyme-controlled reactions such as respiration run faster and make more gas, as the warm and cold yeast results showed. Cold water slows the enzymes and reduces bubbles.
records.new: The gas in the bubbles escapes from the leaf through stomata, microscopic pores in the leaf surface (mostly on the lower side) — which is why bubbles appear at specific spots and not over the whole leaf — and also from the cut edge. Guard cells open each pore when K+ ions enter and water follows by osmosis, making them turgid. Most of the gas was air that was already inside the leaf's air spaces, plus some air dissolved in the water. Leaf cells also make gases: carbon dioxide from respiration in the mitochondria (aerobic respiration gives about 36 to 38 ATP per glucose) and, if the leaf is lit, oxygen from photosynthesis in the chloroplasts. But these processes work over minutes, so they change the mix of gases in the leaf only slowly. We did not test the gas from the leaf directly, so 'mostly air' is our best explanation from the evidence of the unit, not a proven fact. Warm water (about 42°C) gave more bubbles than cold water (about 15°C) within seconds because warming makes the air in the leaf expand and makes the water hold less dissolved gas, so more gas is pushed out; cold water does this much less. Warmth also speeds up enzymes, so respiration in yeast and in leaf cells runs faster, as the warm and cold yeast results showed, but that effect builds up more slowly.

records.why: STORYLINE DECISION to confirm (touches Lessons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 and the Final Explanation). The old lessons said the Lesson 1 bubbles were respiration CO2 and/or photosynthesis O2, made faster in warm water by enzymes, and the Final Explanation then hedged. A leaf in warm water starts to bubble within seconds, but the class's own yeast data show respiration takes minutes to give a clear result, so those processes cannot be the main source. The revised storyline says: most of the gas is air already in the leaf's air spaces (and dissolved in the water); warm water expands it and holds less dissolved gas, so it is pushed out quickly through stomata and cut edges; respiration and photosynthesis change the O2/CO2 mix only slowly; the gas itself was not tested. This also reconciles the two warm-water framings (stomatal opening in Lessons 2-3 and enzyme rates in Lessons 4-12): both are real, but they act over minutes, and the quick effect is physical. Lesson 1 now has a no-leaf control beaker, Lesson 8 has a balloon demonstration, and Lesson 10 has a shared petroleum-jelly investigation. If a teacher prefers to test the gas directly instead, a gas-collection set-up could be added in Lesson 10. The anchoring phenomenon and driving question are unchanged.
